passages.title: The Owl and the Pussy-cat
passages.text:
The Owl and the Pussy-cat went to sea
In a beautiful pea-green boat,
They took some honey, and plenty of money,
Wrapped up in a five-pound note.
The Owl looked up to the stars above,
And sang to a small guitar,
"O lovely Pussy! O Pussy, my love,
What a beautiful Pussy you are,
You are,
You are!
What a beautiful Pussy you are!"

Pussy said to the Owl, "You elegant fowl!
How charmingly sweet you sing!
O let us be married! too long we have tarried:
But what shall we do for a ring?"
They sailed away, for a year and a day,
To the land where the Bong-Tree grows
And there in a wood a Piggy-wig stood
With a ring at the end of his nose,
His nose,
His nose,
With a ring at the end of his nose.

"Dear Pig, are you willing to sell for one shilling
Your ring?" Said the Piggy, "I will."
So they took it away, and were married next day
By the Turkey who lives on the hill.
They dined on mince, and slices of quince,
Which they ate with a runcible spoon;
And hand in hand, on the edge of the sand,
They danced by the light of the moon,
The moon,
The moon,
They danced by the light of the moon.
passages.source_note: Public domain: 'The Owl and the Pussy-cat' by Edward Lear (1871).

questions.stem: What colour was the boat the Owl and the Pussy-cat sailed away in?
questions.explanation: The poem describes 'a beautiful pea-green boat'.

questions.stem: What did the Owl and the Pussy-cat take with them to sea?
questions.explanation: They 'took some honey, and plenty of money, wrapped up in a five-pound note'.

questions.stem: Who married the Owl and the Pussy-cat?

options.text: the Turkey who lives on the hill

questions.explanation: They were 'married next day by the Turkey who lives on the hill'.

questions.stem: Where did the Piggy-wig keep the ring?

options.text: at the end of his nose

questions.explanation: The Piggy-wig stood 'with a ring at the end of his nose'.

questions.stem: The poem tells its story in three sections of several lines each. Each section is called:
questions.explanation: A 'stanza' is a group of lines forming one section of a poem, like a paragraph in prose.

questions.stem: Which pair of words from the poem rhyme with each other?
questions.explanation: 'How charmingly sweet you sing!' rhymes with 'what shall we do for a ring?' -- sing and ring.

questions.stem: At the end of each stanza a short line is repeated three times, such as 'They danced by the light of the moon'. A repeated line like this is called:
questions.explanation: A line brought back again and again, especially to close a verse, is a 'refrain'.

questions.stem: The Owl sings the words 'You are' over and over. This repetition mainly makes his song sound:

options.text: eager and sincere, as if declaring true love

questions.explanation: Repeating 'You are' makes the Owl's declaration of love sound insistent and sincere.

questions.stem: The poem has a strong, bouncing rhythm. This suits it because it:

options.text: makes the poem sound sad and serious
makes the poem feel merry and musical to read aloud
makes the poem hard to read
hides the meaning of the story

questions.explanation: The lively, sing-song beat matches the poem's playful mood and invites reading it aloud.

questions.stem: Which night-time image does the poem paint in the first stanza?

options.text: the Piggy-wig standing in a shady wood
the two friends dancing on the sand
the Owl looking up at the stars above the sea
the Turkey standing on a green hill
a feast of mince and slices of quince

questions.explanation: In the first stanza the Owl 'looked up to the stars above' and sang to a small guitar from the boat.

questions.stem: The picture of the two animals setting off 'in a beautiful pea-green boat' helps to create a mood that is:
questions.explanation: An owl and a cat sailing off together in a brightly coloured boat is charming and fanciful, setting a light, dreamlike tone.

questions.stem: This poem is best described as a narrative poem because it:

options.text: tells a story from beginning to end
is simply a list of rhyming words
repeats one image over and over

questions.explanation: A narrative poem tells a story, and this one follows the pair from setting sail to their wedding dance.

questions.stem: Pussy calls the Owl an 'elegant fowl'. Here a 'fowl' is:
questions.explanation: A 'fowl' is a bird -- fitting, since the Owl is one.

questions.stem: In 'too long we have tarried', the word 'tarried' means:
questions.explanation: To 'tarry' is to delay or wait; Pussy feels they have put off marrying for too long.

questions.stem: They ate 'slices of quince'. A quince is:

options.text: a hard, yellow fruit similar to a pear

questions.explanation: A quince is a hard, yellow fruit rather like a pear.

questions.stem: They ate with a 'runcible spoon'. The word 'runcible' is unusual because it:

options.text: is an old word meaning very large
is an old word for silver
is an old word for wooden
is a made-up word the poet invented, with no fixed meaning

questions.explanation: Edward Lear invented 'runcible' himself; it has no real dictionary meaning and is part of the poem's nonsense fun.

questions.stem: When Pussy asks 'what shall we do for a ring?', it is because they:

options.text: want to get married but have no ring
have lost a ring at sea
want to sell a ring for money
need a ring to steer the boat
were asked for a ring by the Owl

questions.explanation: Pussy has just proposed marriage, and the pair realise they have no ring for the wedding.

questions.stem: What do the Owl's song and words tell us about his feelings for Pussy?

options.text: he loves and admires her deeply
he is a little afraid of her

questions.explanation: Calling her 'lovely' and 'beautiful' and serenading her on the guitar shows deep affection.

questions.stem: How do we know the Piggy-wig agreed to sell the ring?

options.text: he runs off into the wood

questions.explanation: When asked to sell his ring for a shilling, the Piggy replies, 'I will.'

questions.stem: Why did the Owl and Pussy-cat sail 'for a year and a day' to the land where the Bong-Tree grows?

options.text: they were lost and could not find land
they were delivering the five-pound note
they were searching for a place and a way to be married
they were visiting the Owl's family

questions.explanation: Having decided to marry, they set off on a long voyage and there found the Piggy with a ring and the Turkey to wed them.

questions.stem: What kind of poem is this?

options.text: a sad poem about lost love
a serious poem about the sea
a frightening poem about wild animals
a poem teaching a strict moral

questions.explanation: From talking animals to a nose-ring wedding, the whole poem is cheerful and comic.

questions.stem: Why does the poet fill the poem with silly, impossible details, such as animals marrying and a Piggy selling his nose-ring?

options.text: to amuse the reader with playful nonsense
to describe how real animals behave
to warn about talking to strangers
to explain how sailing boats work

questions.explanation: The impossible details are there purely for fun -- this is a nonsense poem meant to delight.

questions.stem: Why might the poet repeat the last line of each stanza three times over?

options.text: to fill up empty space on the page
to make the poem harder to remember
to hide how the story ends
to give each verse a musical, chant-along ending that is fun to say aloud
to show that the characters are bored

questions.explanation: The triple repetition works like the refrain of a song, giving each stanza a catchy, musical close.

questions.stem: Throughout the poem the Owl and the Pussy-cat talk, sing, fall in love and marry. The poet is using:
questions.explanation: Giving animals human qualities and actions is personification.

questions.stem: At the very end of the poem, the Owl and the Pussy-cat:

options.text: set sail in the pea-green boat
dance together on the sand in the moonlight
buy the ring from the Piggy-wig

questions.explanation: The poem closes with the newly-married pair dancing hand in hand on the sand.
